questions.question: Which compound is the major product of the reaction between 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH3)2C=CHCH3, and hydrogen bromide? A 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, B 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, C 1-bromo-2-methylbutane, D 1-bromo-3-methylbutane.
questions.answer: A: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane
steps: HBr adds across the C=C by electrophilic addition: H+ bonds to one alkene carbon and Br- to the other.

H+ adds to the CH carbon, leaving the tertiary carbocation (CH3)2C+CH2CH3. This is more stable than the secondary carbocation formed if H+ added to the C(CH3)2 carbon, because three electron-releasing alkyl groups stabilise the positive charge.
Br- then attacks the tertiary carbocation to give 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (A).
B comes from the less stable secondary carbocation, so it is only the minor product. C and D put Br on a terminal CH3 carbon that is not part of the C=C, so they cannot form.

questions.question: Ethane reacts with bromine in ultraviolet light. Which equation represents a termination step? A Br2 -> 2Br•, B C2H6 + Br• -> C2H5• + HBr, C C2H5• + Br• -> C2H5Br, D C2H5• + Br2 -> C2H5Br + Br•.
questions.answer: C: C2H5• + Br• -> C2H5Br
steps: A termination step uses up two radicals and does not make a new one, so the chain stops.
A is initiation: homolytic fission of Br2 by ultraviolet light.
B and D are propagation steps: each uses one radical and produces another.
C joins two radicals to give a stable molecule, so it is termination.

questions.question: A gaseous hydrocarbon X contains 85.7% carbon by mass. A 0.560 g sample of X occupies 240 cm^3 at room temperature and pressure. Calculate the molar mass of X and hence deduce its molecular formula. [Molar volume of a gas at room temperature and pressure = 24.0 dm^3 mol^-1; H = 1.0, C = 12.0]
questions.answer: Molar mass = 56.0 g mol^-1; X is C4H8
steps: Molar mass = 0.560 g / 0.0100 mol = 56.0 g mol^-1
Carbon in one mole = 0.857 x 56.0 = 48.0 g, which is 4 carbon atoms; hydrogen = 56.0 - 48.0 = 8.0 g, which is 8 hydrogen atoms
Molecular formula = C4H8

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of the reaction between ethene and bromine, C2H4 + Br2 -> CH2BrCH2Br. Your answer should refer to the polarisation of the bromine molecule, the movement of electrons shown by curly arrows, the intermediate formed and the type of bond fission.
questions.answer: Electrophilic addition: the pi electrons attack the polarised Br-Br; heterolytic fission gives a carbocation and Br-; Br- then attacks the carbocation to give 1,2-dibromoethane.
steps: The electron-rich C=C repels the electrons in the Br-Br bond of an approaching molecule, inducing a dipole: the nearer Br atom becomes delta+ (1 mark).
A curly arrow from the C=C double bond to the delta+ Br atom shows the pi electrons forming a new C-Br bond (1 mark).
A curly arrow from the Br-Br bond to the further Br atom shows heterolytic fission, giving Br- and a carbocation intermediate, +CH2CH2Br (1 mark).
A curly arrow from a lone pair on Br- to the C+ forms the second C-Br bond, giving 1,2-dibromoethane (1 mark).

questions.question: In ultraviolet light, methane reacts with chlorine to form chloromethane, CH3Cl. The product mixture also contains CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4. Explain why these further products form and suggest how the proportion of chloromethane in the product mixture can be increased.
questions.answer: Chloromethane still has C-H bonds, so Cl• radicals can substitute more hydrogen atoms; use a large excess of methane.
steps: Chloromethane still contains C-H bonds, so a Cl• radical can remove an H atom: CH3Cl + Cl• -> •CH2Cl + HCl.
The •CH2Cl radical reacts with Cl2 to give CH2Cl2 and a new Cl•, so the chain continues and hydrogen atoms are replaced one at a time, up to CCl4.
Using a large excess of methane makes it more likely that a Cl• radical collides with a CH4 molecule rather than a chloromethane molecule, so mainly chloromethane forms.

questions.question: 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, is a gas used to make polymers. Explain why 2-methylpropene does not show E-Z isomerism.
questions.answer: Each carbon of the C=C carries two identical groups (H and H on one, CH3 and CH3 on the other), so there are no different arrangements of groups about the double bond.
steps: E-Z isomerism needs restricted rotation about the C=C and two different groups on each carbon atom of the double bond.
The CH2 carbon carries two H atoms and the other carbon carries two CH3 groups, so swapping groups on either carbon gives the same molecule.

questions.question: 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, reacts with hydrogen bromide to form mainly one product. Name this major product and explain, in terms of the intermediate formed, why it is the major product.
questions.answer: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CBr, formed through the more stable tertiary carbocation (CH3)3C+
steps: H+ adds to the CH2 carbon, giving the tertiary carbocation (CH3)3C+. Adding H+ to the other carbon would give the primary carbocation (CH3)2CHCH2+.
Alkyl groups release electrons, so three alkyl groups stabilise the positive charge in the tertiary carbocation more than the single alkyl group does in the primary carbocation.
The more stable carbocation forms faster, so most of the product comes from it: Br- attacks (CH3)3C+ to give 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

questions.question: 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, forms a polymer by addition polymerisation. Give the repeat unit of poly(2-methylpropene) and calculate the number of monomer units in a polymer chain of relative molecular mass 2.80 x 10^5. [H = 1.0, C = 12.0]
questions.answer: Repeat unit -CH2-C(CH3)2-; 5.00 x 10^3 monomer units
steps: The C=C opens, so the repeat unit is -CH2-C(CH3)2-, which has the same formula as the monomer, C4H8.
Number of monomer units = 280000 / 56.0 = 5.00 x 10^3

questions.question: Equal amounts of four 1-halogenobutanes are warmed separately with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol. Which compound produces a precipitate fastest? A 1-fluorobutane, B 1-chlorobutane, C 1-bromobutane, D 1-iodobutane.
questions.answer: D: 1-iodobutane
steps: A precipitate of silver halide forms when the C-X bond is broken by hydrolysis and the halide ion reacts with Ag+.
The rate depends on the strength of the C-X bond, not on its polarity. The C-I bond is the weakest, so it breaks most easily and yellow AgI forms fastest (D).
C-F is the most polar bond but also the strongest, so 1-fluorobutane gives no visible precipitate (A). C-Cl (B) and C-Br (C) are both stronger than C-I, so they react more slowly.

questions.question: 2-bromopentane, CH3CHBrCH2CH2CH3, is heated under reflux with ethanolic potassium hydroxide. How many different alkenes, counting E and Z isomers separately, can form? A 1, B 2, C 3, D 4.
questions.answer: C: 3 (pent-1-ene, E-pent-2-ene and Z-pent-2-ene)
steps: Ethanolic KOH causes elimination of HBr: H is removed from a carbon next to the carbon bonded to Br.
Removing H from C1 (the CH3 group) gives pent-1-ene, CH2=CHCH2CH2CH3.
Removing H from C3 (the CH2 group) gives pent-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH2CH3, which exists as E and Z isomers. Total = 1 + 2 = 3 (C).
A and B miss one or more of these products. D is impossible because only two carbons next to C2 carry hydrogen atoms.

questions.question: Propan-1-ol can be oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate(VI) to give either propanal or propanoic acid. State the conditions that favour each product and explain why they work.
questions.answer: Propanal: warm gently with excess alcohol and distil the product off as it forms. Propanoic acid: excess oxidising agent and heat under reflux.
steps: For propanal, add the oxidising agent to excess propan-1-ol, warm gently and distil off the propanal as it forms (1 mark).
Propanal has a lower boiling temperature than propan-1-ol or propanoic acid because it cannot form hydrogen bonds, so it leaves the flask before it can be oxidised further (1 mark).
For propanoic acid, use excess acidified dichromate(VI) and heat under reflux so that the aldehyde stays in the flask and is fully oxidised (1 mark).

questions.question: 1-bromobutane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide mainly by the SN2 mechanism, but 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts mainly by the SN1 mechanism. Explain, with reference to the structures of the halogenoalkanes, the steps in each mechanism and the rate equations, why the two compounds react differently.
questions.answer: Primary 1-bromobutane: unhindered, one-step SN2, rate = k[RBr][OH-]. Tertiary 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: hindered but gives a stable carbocation, two-step SN1, rate = k[RBr].
steps: 1-bromobutane is a primary halogenoalkane: the carbon bonded to Br is not crowded, so OH- can attack it directly from the side opposite the Br (1 mark).
A primary carbocation would be unstable, so SN2 occurs in one step through a transition state in which OH- is partly bonded to carbon as the C-Br bond breaks (1 mark).
In SN2 both the halogenoalkane and OH- are involved in the rate-determining step, so rate = k[C4H9Br][OH-]: second order overall (1 mark).
2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary: the three CH3 groups block attack by OH-, and electron-releasing alkyl groups stabilise the carbocation (CH3)3C+ (1 mark).
The C-Br bond breaks first in a slow step to give (CH3)3C+ and Br-, then OH- attacks quickly. Rate = k[(CH3)3CBr]: first order and independent of [OH-] (1 mark).

questions.question: 0.0500 mol of 1-bromobutane is heated under reflux with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide until all of it has reacted. The mixture is cooled and acidified with dilute nitric acid, and excess aqueous silver nitrate is added. (i) State the colour of the precipitate formed and name it. (ii) Explain why the mixture is acidified with nitric acid before the silver nitrate is added. (iii) Calculate the maximum mass of precipitate formed. [Ag = 107.9, Br = 79.9]
questions.answer: (i) Cream precipitate of silver bromide. (ii) To remove excess OH-, which would form a brown precipitate with Ag+. (iii) 9.39 g
steps: C4H9Br + OH- -> C4H9OH + Br-. One mole of halogenoalkane releases one mole of Br-, which forms AgBr: Ag+ + Br- -> AgBr. The precipitate is cream.
Nitric acid neutralises the excess OH-. Without it Ag+ would react with OH- to form a brown precipitate of silver(I) oxide that hides the result.

questions.question: Ethanol is made industrially by the hydration of ethene and also by the fermentation of glucose. Write the equation for the hydration of ethene to form ethanol and state the catalyst and the temperature and pressure used in the industrial process.
questions.answer: C2H4 + H2O <=> C2H5OH; phosphoric acid catalyst; about 300 °C and 60-70 atm
steps: Equation: C2H4(g) + H2O(g) <=> C2H5OH(g), using a reversible arrow (1 mark).
Catalyst: phosphoric acid, H3PO4, usually supported on silica (1 mark).
Conditions: about 300 °C and a pressure of 60-70 atm (1 mark).

questions.question: Ethanol can be made by the fermentation of glucose: C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2. Calculate the percentage atom economy for the formation of ethanol by this reaction. [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0]
steps: Mr of ethanol, C2H5OH = 46.0, so the mass of ethanol in the equation = 2 x 46.0 = 92.0

questions.question: Ethanol is made by fermentation of glucose and by the hydration of ethene. Evaluate the use of fermentation compared with hydration of ethene for the large-scale production of ethanol, considering the raw materials, the reaction conditions, the type of process and the purity of the product.
questions.answer: Fermentation is renewable and uses mild conditions but is slow, batch and gives dilute ethanol with a 51% atom economy; hydration is fast, continuous, pure and 100% atom economic but uses finite crude oil and high temperature and pressure.
steps: Raw materials: fermentation uses sugars from plants, which are renewable; hydration uses ethene from crude oil, which is finite.
Conditions: fermentation works at about 30-40 °C and atmospheric pressure, so it needs little energy; hydration needs about 300 °C and 60-70 atm, which is energy intensive.
Type of process: fermentation is slow and a batch process; hydration is fast and continuous, giving a high output.
Product: fermentation gives a dilute ethanol solution that needs fractional distillation; hydration gives a purer product, with atom economy of 100% against 51% for fermentation.
Any four of these points earn the 4 marks, including a reasoned overall judgement, for example that fermentation is more sustainable but hydration is more efficient and economic at large scale.

questions.question: Which reagent can be used to distinguish pentan-2-one from pentan-3-one? A 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, B Tollens' reagent, C iodine in aqueous sodium hydroxide, D acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
questions.answer: C: iodine in aqueous sodium hydroxide
steps: Pentan-2-one, CH3COCH2CH2CH3, contains the CH3C=O group, so it gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane (CHI3) with iodine and sodium hydroxide.
Pentan-3-one, CH3CH2COCH2CH3, has no CH3C=O group, so there is no precipitate.

A is wrong because both ketones give an orange precipitate. B is wrong because neither ketone gives a silver mirror. D is wrong because ketones are not oxidised by dichromate(VI), so both stay orange.

questions.question: Which pair of compounds, heated with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid, forms propyl ethanoate? A ethanoic acid and propan-2-ol, B propanoic acid and ethanol, C ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol, D propanoic acid and propan-1-ol.
questions.answer: C: ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol
steps: In the name of an ester the first word comes from the alcohol (propyl, from propan-1-ol) and the second word from the acid (ethanoate, from ethanoic acid).
So ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol give CH3COOCH2CH2CH3, propyl ethanoate (C).
A would give the isomer propan-2-yl ethanoate, B would give ethyl propanoate, and D would give propyl propanoate.

questions.question: Describe how Tollens' reagent can be used to distinguish propanal from propanone. Give the observation with each compound and state what happens to the silver ions.
questions.answer: Propanal gives a silver mirror; propanone gives no change; Ag+ is reduced to Ag.
steps: Add a few drops of each compound to Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate, containing [Ag(NH3)2]+) and warm gently in a water bath.
Propanal, an aldehyde, is oxidised to propanoic acid (propanoate) and a silver mirror forms on the inside of the tube. Propanone, a ketone, is not oxidised, so there is no change.
The silver ions are reduced: Ag+ + e- -> Ag.

questions.question: A carboxylic acid X contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. Complete combustion of 0.370 g of X gives 0.660 g of carbon dioxide and 0.270 g of water. The relative molecular mass of X is 74.0. Calculate the empirical formula of X, deduce its molecular formula and name X. [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0]
questions.answer: Empirical formula C3H6O2; molecular formula C3H6O2; X is propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH
steps: Mass of O = 0.370 - 0.180 - 0.0300 = 0.160 g, so n(O) = 0.0100 mol. Ratio C : H : O = 0.0150 : 0.0300 : 0.0100 = 3 : 6 : 2, so the empirical formula is C3H6O2 (Mr 74.0)
The empirical formula mass equals the relative molecular mass, so the molecular formula is C3H6O2. As X is a carboxylic acid it is CH3CH2COOH, propanoic acid.

questions.question: Ethanal, CH3CHO, reacts with hydrogen cyanide to form 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, CH3CH(OH)CN. State the type of reaction and explain why the carbon atom of the C=O group in ethanal is attacked by the cyanide ion.
questions.answer: Nucleophilic addition; the C=O carbon is delta+ because oxygen is more electronegative, so it is attacked by the nucleophile CN-.
steps: The reaction is nucleophilic addition: CN- adds across the C=O double bond.
Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C=O bond is polar and the carbon is delta+.
CN- is a nucleophile (it donates a lone pair of electrons), so it attacks the electron-deficient carbon atom.

questions.question: Ethanal, CH3CHO, can be converted into 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, CH3CH(OH)CN. Give the reagents used to carry out this conversion in the laboratory and state the role of each.
questions.answer: Potassium cyanide, KCN, supplies CN- ions as the nucleophile; dilute acid (for example sulfuric acid) supplies H+ ions to protonate the intermediate.
steps: Aqueous potassium cyanide, KCN, supplies a high concentration of CN- ions, the nucleophile (HCN alone is a weak acid and gives very few CN- ions).
Dilute acid, for example sulfuric acid, supplies H+ ions that protonate the O- of the intermediate anion to form the -OH group of the product.

questions.question: Ethanal, CH3CHO, reacts with hydrogen cyanide to form 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, CH3CH(OH)CN, with the equation CH3CHO + HCN -> CH3CH(OH)CN. Calculate the maximum mass of 2-hydroxypropanenitrile that can be made from 4.40 g of ethanal. [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, N = 14.0, O = 16.0]
steps: The equation is 1 : 1, so the maximum amount of product is 0.100 mol. Mr of CH3CH(OH)CN = 3 x 12.0 + 5 x 1.0 + 14.0 + 16.0 = 71.0
Maximum mass = 0.100 x 71.0 = 7.10 g

questions.question: Ethanal reacts with cyanide ions and acid to form 2-hydroxypropanenitrile, CH3CH(OH)CN, whose molecules are chiral. Explain why the product made in this reaction has no effect on plane-polarised light.
questions.answer: The planar C=O is attacked from either side with equal probability, so equal amounts of the two enantiomers form (a racemic mixture) and their effects on plane-polarised light cancel.
steps: CH3CH(OH)CN has a chiral centre: the carbon bonded to four different groups (H, CH3, OH and CN).
The C=O group and the atoms bonded to it are planar, so CN- can attack from above or below the plane with equal probability.
Equal amounts of the two non-superimposable mirror-image forms (enantiomers) form, a racemic mixture. Their rotations of plane-polarised light cancel, so the mixture is optically inactive.

questions.question: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene to cyclohexane is -120 kJ mol^-1. The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of benzene to cyclohexane is -208 kJ mol^-1. Compared with a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene that has three localised C=C bonds, benzene is A 152 kJ mol^-1 less stable, B 152 kJ mol^-1 more stable, C 88 kJ mol^-1 more stable, D 240 kJ mol^-1 more stable.
questions.answer: B: benzene is 152 kJ mol^-1 more stable
steps: If benzene had three localised C=C bonds, hydrogenation would release about 3 x (-120) = -360 kJ mol^-1.
The measured value is -208 kJ mol^-1, which is 360 - 208 = 152 kJ mol^-1 less exothermic.
Less energy is released because benzene starts at a lower energy, so benzene is 152 kJ mol^-1 more stable owing to delocalisation (B).
A has the sign reversed. C comes from 208 - 120 and D from 360 - 120, which are both invalid comparisons.

questions.question: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous aluminium chloride to form phenylethanone, C6H5COCH3. Which species is the electrophile that attacks the benzene ring? A CH3COCl, B CH3CO+, C Cl+, D AlCl4-.
questions.answer: B: CH3CO+
steps: Aluminium chloride accepts a lone pair from the chlorine of ethanoyl chloride: CH3COCl + AlCl3 -> CH3CO+ + AlCl4-.
CH3CO+ is positively charged and electron deficient, so it attacks the delocalised pi electrons of the ring: it is the electrophile (B).
CH3COCl (A) is the reactant, not the attacking species. Cl+ (C) is not formed in this reaction. AlCl4- (D) is the negative ion that later removes H+ and regenerates AlCl3.

questions.question: Benzene is nitrated by a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid at about 50 °C. (i) Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile in this mixture. (ii) Explain why the sulfuric acid is described as a catalyst. (iii) Give a reason why the temperature must not rise much above 55 °C.
questions.answer: (i) HNO3 + H2SO4 -> NO2+ + HSO4- + H2O; (ii) it is regenerated in the final step (H+ + HSO4- -> H2SO4); (iii) above 55 °C further nitration gives dinitrobenzene.
steps: (i) The electrophile is the nitronium ion: HNO3 + H2SO4 -> NO2+ + HSO4- + H2O (1 mark).
(ii) The H+ lost from the ring in the last step reacts with HSO4-: H+ + HSO4- -> H2SO4, so the sulfuric acid is regenerated and is not used up (1 mark).
(iii) At higher temperatures a second NO2 group is substituted, giving dinitrobenzene as an unwanted product (1 mark).

questions.question: Phenol reacts with aqueous bromine at room temperature, but benzene does not react with bromine under the same conditions. State what is seen when excess bromine water is added to phenol and explain the difference in reactivity.
questions.answer: The bromine water is decolourised and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms; the lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring, making it more electron rich and more reactive than benzene.
steps: Observation: the orange bromine water is decolourised and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms (1 mark).
In phenol a lone pair on the oxygen atom overlaps with and is delocalised into the pi system of the ring, increasing the electron density of the ring, especially at positions 2, 4 and 6 (1 mark).

The more electron-rich ring polarises Br2 more strongly, so substitution occurs without a halogen carrier. Benzene has a lower electron density, so it needs a catalyst such as FeBr3 or AlBr3 (1 mark).

questions.question: Cyclohexene decolourises bromine water at room temperature by addition, but benzene reacts with bromine only in the presence of a halogen carrier such as iron(III) bromide, and it gives a substitution product. Explain these differences in terms of the structure and bonding in the two molecules.
questions.answer: Cyclohexene has a localised, electron-rich C=C that polarises Br2; benzene has delocalised pi electrons, so it needs a halogen carrier to make a stronger electrophile and it undergoes substitution to keep the delocalised ring.
steps: In cyclohexene the pi electrons are localised between two carbon atoms, giving a high electron density that polarises Br2, so no catalyst is needed (1 mark).
In benzene the six pi electrons are delocalised over the whole ring, so the electron density between any two carbons is lower and benzene cannot polarise Br2 enough to react (1 mark).
A halogen carrier (FeBr3 or AlBr3) accepts a lone pair from Br2 to generate a much stronger electrophile, Br+ (1 mark).
Addition to benzene would destroy the delocalised system and lose its extra stability of about 150 kJ mol^-1 (1 mark).
Substitution of H by Br keeps the delocalised ring, giving bromobenzene and HBr (1 mark).

questions.question: Phenylethanone, C6H5COCH3, can be made from benzene in one step. Give the reagents and conditions for this reaction.
questions.answer: Ethanoyl chloride, CH3COCl, with anhydrous aluminium chloride as catalyst, heated under reflux in dry conditions
steps: Reagent: ethanoyl chloride, CH3COCl (1 mark).
Catalyst and conditions: anhydrous aluminium chloride, AlCl3, under dry conditions with heating under reflux (1 mark).

questions.question: Benzene is converted into phenylethanone, C6H5COCH3, using ethanoyl chloride and anhydrous aluminium chloride. Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile from ethanoyl chloride and aluminium chloride.
questions.answer: CH3COCl + AlCl3 -> CH3CO+ + AlCl4-
steps: Aluminium chloride accepts a lone pair of electrons from the chlorine atom of ethanoyl chloride. The C-Cl bond breaks to form the acylium ion CH3CO+ and AlCl4-.

questions.question: Benzene is converted into phenylethanone, C6H5COCH3, using ethanoyl chloride and anhydrous aluminium chloride. In the final step of the mechanism a hydrogen ion is lost from the ring. Write an equation to show how the catalyst is regenerated.
questions.answer: AlCl4- + H+ -> AlCl3 + HCl
steps: The H+ lost from the intermediate combines with AlCl4- to regenerate the catalyst AlCl3 and to form the by-product HCl.

questions.question: Phenylethanone, C6H5COCH3, is warmed with a solution of iodine in aqueous sodium hydroxide. Name the organic compound that forms as a yellow precipitate and the organic compound that remains in solution.
questions.answer: Yellow precipitate: triiodomethane, CHI3. In solution: sodium benzoate, C6H5COONa
steps: Phenylethanone contains the CH3C=O group, so it gives the triiodomethane (iodoform) reaction.
C6H5COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> C6H5COONa + CHI3 + 3NaI + 3H2O, so the precipitate is CHI3 and the organic compound left in solution is sodium benzoate.

questions.question: Which compound is the strongest base? A ammonia, NH3, B ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2, C phenylamine, C6H5NH2, D ethanamide, CH3CONH2.
questions.answer: B: ethylamine
steps: Basic strength depends on how available the lone pair on nitrogen is to accept H+.
In ethylamine the electron-releasing ethyl group increases the electron density on N, so its lone pair accepts H+ more readily than the lone pair in ammonia.
In phenylamine the lone pair is partly delocalised into the benzene ring, and in ethanamide it is delocalised towards the C=O group, so both are much weaker bases than ammonia.

questions.question: Which procedure converts bromoethane into propan-1-amine, CH3CH2CH2NH2? A heat with excess ethanolic ammonia in a sealed tube, B heat under reflux with ethanolic potassium cyanide and then reduce the product with LiAlH4 in dry ether, C heat under reflux with ethanolic potassium cyanide and then heat the product under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid, D heat under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide and then react the product with ammonia.
questions.answer: B: KCN then LiAlH4 in dry ether
steps: Propan-1-amine has one more carbon than bromoethane, so a carbon atom must be added: KCN gives CH3CH2CN (propanenitrile).
Reducing the nitrile with LiAlH4 in dry ether gives CH3CH2CH2NH2 (B).
A gives ethylamine, which has only two carbons. C gives propanoic acid after hydrolysis of the nitrile. D gives ethanol, which does not react with ammonia in this way.

questions.question: Alanine is an amino acid with the structure CH3CH(NH2)COOH. Give the structural formula of the form of alanine that predominates (i) in the solid state, (ii) in strongly acidic solution, (iii) in strongly alkaline solution.
questions.answer: (i) CH3CH(NH3+)COO- (zwitterion); (ii) CH3CH(NH3+)COOH; (iii) CH3CH(NH2)COO-
steps: (i) In the solid state the COOH group donates H+ to the NH2 group to give the zwitterion CH3CH(NH3+)COO- (1 mark).
(ii) In strongly acidic solution the carboxylate group is protonated, so the ion is CH3CH(NH3+)COOH (1 mark).
(iii) In strongly alkaline solution the NH3+ group loses H+, so the ion is CH3CH(NH2)COO- (1 mark).

questions.question: Bromoethane reacts with ammonia in ethanol to form ethylamine, but the product also contains diethylamine and triethylamine. Explain why these other amines form and state how the proportion of ethylamine can be increased.
questions.answer: Ethylamine is also a nucleophile, so it reacts with more bromoethane; use a large excess of ammonia.
steps: Ethylamine has a lone pair on nitrogen, so it is also a nucleophile and can attack another molecule of bromoethane (1 mark).
This gives diethylamine, which can react again to give triethylamine and then a quaternary ammonium salt (1 mark).
Using a large excess of ammonia makes it much more likely that bromoethane collides with an ammonia molecule rather than with an amine, so mainly ethylamine forms (1 mark).

questions.question: An amino acid Y contains 40.4% carbon, 7.9% hydrogen, 15.7% nitrogen and 36.0% oxygen by mass. Its relative molecular mass is 89.0. Calculate the empirical formula and the molecular formula of Y, and name Y given that it is a 2-amino acid. [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, N = 14.0, O = 16.0]
questions.answer: Empirical formula C3H7NO2; molecular formula C3H7NO2; Y is 2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine)
steps: Dividing by the smallest (1.12) gives C : H : N : O = 3 : 7 : 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is C3H7NO2 (Mr 89.0)
This equals the relative molecular mass, so the molecular formula is C3H7NO2. As a 2-amino acid, Y is CH3CH(NH2)COOH, 2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine).

questions.question: Phenylamine can be converted into an azo dye in two steps, by way of benzenediazonium chloride. State the reagents and conditions used to convert phenylamine into benzenediazonium chloride and explain why the temperature must be controlled.
questions.answer: Sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid, below 10 °C (0-5 °C); at a higher temperature the diazonium ion decomposes.
steps: Reagents: sodium nitrite (NaNO2) and hydrochloric acid, which react to form nitrous acid, HNO2, in the mixture (1 mark).
Temperature: below 10 °C, usually 0-5 °C, using an ice bath (1 mark).
Above this temperature the diazonium ion decomposes, forming phenol and nitrogen gas (1 mark).

questions.question: Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with a solution of phenol in aqueous sodium hydroxide to form an azo compound. Give the structural formula of the organic product.
questions.answer: HO-C6H4-N=N-C6H5 (4-hydroxyazobenzene, with the azo group para to the OH group)
steps: The diazonium ion attacks the activated ring of the phenoxide ion, mainly at position 4 (para to the OH group), replacing an H atom.
Product: C6H5-N=N-C6H4-OH, 4-hydroxyazobenzene (an orange or yellow dye).

questions.question: Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with a solution of phenol in aqueous sodium hydroxide to form an azo compound. Name the type of reaction that forms the azo compound.
questions.answer: A coupling reaction (electrophilic substitution on the ring of phenol)
steps: The diazonium ion acts as the electrophile and couples with the activated aromatic ring, so the reaction is a coupling reaction.

questions.question: Benzenediazonium chloride couples with phenol to form 4-hydroxyazobenzene, HO-C6H4-N=N-C6H5, which is coloured. Explain why azo compounds such as this are coloured.
questions.answer: The N=N group links two benzene rings so the delocalised system extends over the whole molecule, lowering the energy gap so that visible light is absorbed.
steps: The -N=N- group joins the two rings, so the delocalised pi electron system extends over the whole molecule.
This lowers the energy gap between electronic energy levels so that light in the visible region is absorbed, and the transmitted light is coloured.

questions.question: Phenol is dissolved in aqueous sodium hydroxide before it is added to benzenediazonium chloride in the coupling reaction. Explain why this is done.
questions.answer: Phenol forms the phenoxide ion, C6H5O-, whose ring is more electron rich and so more reactive towards the weakly electrophilic diazonium ion.
steps: Sodium hydroxide removes H+ from phenol to form the phenoxide ion, C6H5O-.
The negative charge on oxygen is delocalised into the ring more strongly than the lone pair in phenol, making the ring more reactive towards the diazonium ion, which is only a weak electrophile.

questions.question: Which compound exists as a pair of optical isomers? A 2-methylbutan-2-ol, B 3-methylpentane, C 2-methylbutan-1-ol, D 2-methylpropan-1-ol.
questions.answer: C: 2-methylbutan-1-ol
steps: Optical isomers occur when a carbon atom is bonded to four different groups.
In 2-methylbutan-1-ol, HOCH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3, carbon 2 is bonded to H, CH3, CH2CH3 and CH2OH, which are all different (C).
In A, B and D no carbon has four different groups: for example in 2-methylpropan-1-ol, HOCH2CH(CH3)2, carbon 2 carries two identical CH3 groups.

questions.question: Which reaction is an example of nucleophilic substitution? A ethene with bromine, B bromoethane with potassium hydroxide in water, C methane with chlorine in ultraviolet light, D benzene with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid.
questions.answer: B: bromoethane with potassium hydroxide in water
steps: In nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile uses a lone pair to replace a group on a carbon atom: CH3CH2Br + OH- -> CH3CH2OH + Br- (B).
A is electrophilic addition, C is free radical substitution and D is electrophilic substitution.

questions.question: Propanoic acid can be made from ethene in three steps. For each step, give the reagent(s) and condition(s) and the structural formula of the organic product.
questions.answer: Step 1: HBr gives CH3CH2Br. Step 2: KCN in aqueous ethanol, heat under reflux, gives CH3CH2CN. Step 3: dilute HCl, heat under reflux, gives CH3CH2COOH.
steps: Step 1: ethene and hydrogen bromide (room temperature) by electrophilic addition give bromoethane, CH3CH2Br.
Step 2: heat under reflux with potassium cyanide in aqueous ethanol (nucleophilic substitution) to give propanenitrile, CH3CH2CN. This step adds the extra carbon atom.
Step 3: heat under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid (or sulfuric acid) to hydrolyse the nitrile to propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH.
One mark for each correct step and one mark for correct organic products at each stage (4 marks in total).

questions.question: A sample containing only one optical isomer of 2-bromobutane, CH3CHBrCH2CH3, is hydrolysed to butan-2-ol with aqueous potassium hydroxide. Explain how the optical activity of the butan-2-ol formed would differ if the reaction took place entirely by (i) the SN1 mechanism and (ii) the SN2 mechanism.
questions.answer: SN1: planar carbocation attacked from either side gives a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive. SN2: attack from the side opposite Br gives a single enantiomer (inverted configuration), which is optically active.
steps: SN1: the C-Br bond breaks first to give a planar carbocation intermediate, CH3CH+CH2CH3 (1 mark).

OH- can attack the planar carbocation from either side with equal probability, so equal amounts of the two enantiomers form (a racemic mixture) (1 mark). The effects on plane-polarised light cancel, so the product is optically inactive.
SN2: OH- attacks the carbon from the side opposite Br in a single step, so the configuration at the chiral carbon is inverted (1 mark).
Only one enantiomer of butan-2-ol forms, so the product remains optically active (1 mark).

questions.question: Compound W has the molecular formula C4H8O. W gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine, no change when warmed with Tollens' reagent, and a yellow precipitate when warmed with iodine and aqueous sodium hydroxide. Deduce the structural formula of W, explaining what each test shows.
questions.answer: W is butanone, CH3COCH2CH3
steps: The orange precipitate with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine shows that W contains a C=O group, so it is an aldehyde or a ketone (1 mark).
No silver mirror with Tollens' reagent shows that W is not an aldehyde, so it is a ketone (1 mark).
The yellow precipitate (CHI3) with iodine and sodium hydroxide shows that W contains the CH3C=O group (1 mark).
The only ketone with formula C4H8O is butanone, CH3COCH2CH3, which does contain a CH3C=O group (1 mark).

questions.question: 1-bromobutane is prepared by heating butan-1-ol under reflux with sodium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid. Write equations for the formation of hydrogen bromide from sodium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid, and for the reaction of hydrogen bromide with butan-1-ol.
questions.answer: NaBr + H2SO4 -> HBr + NaHSO4; CH3CH2CH2CH2OH + HBr -> CH3CH2CH2CH2Br + H2O
steps: Sodium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid produce hydrogen bromide: NaBr + H2SO4 -> HBr + NaHSO4 (1 mark).
Hydrogen bromide substitutes the OH group of the alcohol: CH3CH2CH2CH2OH + HBr -> CH3CH2CH2CH2Br + H2O (1 mark).

questions.question: 1-bromobutane is prepared by heating butan-1-ol under reflux with sodium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid. Describe how a pure, dry sample of 1-bromobutane is obtained from the reaction mixture after reflux. (1-bromobutane is denser than water and boils at about 102 °C.)
questions.answer: Distil off the crude product, wash with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in a separating funnel, run off the lower organic layer, dry with an anhydrous drying agent and redistil, collecting the fraction at about 102 °C.
steps: Distil the reaction mixture and collect the distillate, which contains crude 1-bromobutane (1 mark).
Shake the distillate with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution in a separating funnel (releasing the pressure) to remove acidic impurities (1 mark).
The lower layer is the denser 1-bromobutane: run it off and discard the aqueous layer, then dry with an anhydrous drying agent such as anhydrous calcium chloride or magnesium sulfate (1 mark).
Decant or filter off the drying agent and redistil, collecting the fraction that boils at about 102 °C (1 mark).

questions.question: In one preparation of 1-bromobutane from butan-1-ol, 10.0 g of butan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH, gave 12.4 g of 1-bromobutane, CH3CH2CH2CH2Br. Calculate the percentage yield. [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, Br = 79.9]
steps: The equation is 1 : 1. Mr of 1-bromobutane = 4 x 12.0 + 9 x 1.0 + 79.9 = 136.9, so the theoretical mass = 0.1351 x 136.9 = 18.5 g
Percentage yield = 12.4 / 18.5 x 100 = 67.0%

questions.question: The mass spectrum of a halogenoalkane has two molecular ion peaks, at m/z 122 and m/z 124, of almost equal height. Which compound gives this pattern? [Isotopes: 79Br and 81Br occur in a ratio of about 1 : 1; 35Cl and 37Cl occur in a ratio of about 3 : 1.] A CH3CH2Br, B CH3CH2CH2Br, C CH3CH2CH2Cl, D CH3CH2CH2CH2Br.
questions.answer: B: CH3CH2CH2Br
steps: Two molecular ion peaks two mass units apart and of equal height show bromine (79Br and 81Br in a ratio of 1 : 1). Chlorine would give a 3 : 1 pattern.
For C3H7Br: 3 x 12 + 7 x 1 + 79 = 122, and with 81Br the peak is at 124 (B).
A would give peaks at 108 and 110, D at 136 and 138, and C at 78 and 80 in a 3 : 1 ratio.

questions.question: The high-resolution 1H NMR spectrum of a compound consists of only two peaks, a doublet and a septet. Which compound gives this spectrum? A CH3CH2CH2Br, B (CH3)2CHBr, C (CH3)3CBr, D CH3CH2Br.
questions.answer: B: (CH3)2CHBr
steps: In (CH3)2CHBr the two CH3 groups are equivalent: their six hydrogens are next to one hydrogen, so they give a doublet (n + 1 = 2).
The single CH hydrogen is next to six equivalent hydrogens, so it gives a septet (n + 1 = 7). B gives only these two peaks.
A gives three peaks (triplet, sextet and triplet), C gives one singlet, and D gives a triplet and a quartet.

questions.question: State the number of peaks in the 13C NMR spectrum of each of these compounds: (i) 2,3-dimethylbutane, (CH3)2CHCH(CH3)2, (ii) 1,4-dimethylbenzene, (iii) propyl ethanoate, CH3COOCH2CH2CH3.
steps: (i) The four CH3 carbons are equivalent and the two CH carbons are equivalent, so there are 2 peaks.
(ii) The two CH3 carbons are equivalent, the two ring carbons bonded to CH3 are equivalent, and the four ring CH carbons are equivalent, so there are 3 peaks.
(iii) All five carbons (CH3CO, C=O, OCH2, CH2 and the end CH3) are in different environments, so there are 5 peaks.

questions.question: Propan-1-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and the organic product is isolated. Describe how the infrared spectrum of the product would show whether it is propanal or propanoic acid. [Absorption ranges: C=O 1680-1750 cm^-1; O-H in alcohols 3200-3550 cm^-1; O-H in carboxylic acids 2500-3300 cm^-1 (broad).]
questions.answer: Both show C=O at 1680-1750 cm^-1. Propanoic acid also shows a very broad O-H absorption at 2500-3300 cm^-1; propanal shows no O-H absorption.
steps: Propanal and propanoic acid both contain C=O, so both have a strong absorption in the range 1680-1750 cm^-1, which cannot tell them apart (1 mark).
Propanoic acid also has a very broad O-H absorption between 2500 and 3300 cm^-1 (1 mark).
Propanal has no O-H group, so there is no O-H absorption. The absence of a band at 3200-3550 cm^-1 also shows that no unreacted propan-1-ol remains (1 mark).

questions.question: Compound E contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. It contains 54.5% carbon and 9.1% hydrogen by mass. The molecular ion peak in the mass spectrum of E is at m/z 88. Show that the molecular formula of E is C4H8O2. [H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0]
questions.answer: Empirical formula C2H4O (Mr 44.0); the molecular ion at m/z 88 gives C4H8O2
steps: Percentage of oxygen = 100 - 54.5 - 9.1 = 36.4%
Empirical formula C2H4O has Mr = 44.0. The molecular ion peak shows Mr = 88, which is 2 x 44.0, so the molecular formula is C4H8O2.

questions.question: Compound E has the molecular formula C4H8O2. Its infrared spectrum has a strong absorption at 1740 cm^-1 and no broad absorptions above 2500 cm^-1. Use the ranges C=O 1680-1750 cm^-1, O-H in carboxylic acids 2500-3300 cm^-1 and O-H in alcohols 3200-3550 cm^-1 to explain what this shows about the functional groups in E.
questions.answer: E contains a C=O group but no O-H group, so it is not an acid or an alcohol; it is an ester.
steps: The absorption at 1740 cm^-1 lies in the C=O range 1680-1750 cm^-1, so E contains a carbonyl group.
There is no broad absorption at 2500-3300 cm^-1 or at 3200-3550 cm^-1, so E has no O-H group and is not a carboxylic acid or an alcohol. With two oxygen atoms and a C=O group, E is an ester.

questions.question: Compound E is an ester with the molecular formula C4H8O2. Its high-resolution 1H NMR spectrum has three peaks: a singlet at 3.7 ppm (relative area 3), a quartet at 2.3 ppm (relative area 2) and a triplet at 1.1 ppm (relative area 3). [Chemical shifts: CH3-C 0.9-1.3 ppm; CH2-C=O 2.1-2.7 ppm; CH3-O 3.3-4.3 ppm.] Deduce the structure of E, explaining the splitting of the quartet and the triplet.
questions.answer: Methyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH3
steps: Singlet at 3.7 ppm, area 3: a CH3 group bonded to oxygen (OCH3) with no hydrogens on the adjacent atom.
Quartet at 2.3 ppm, area 2: a CH2 group next to C=O, split into four peaks by the three hydrogens of the neighbouring CH3 (n + 1 = 4).
Triplet at 1.1 ppm, area 3: a CH3 group split into three by the two hydrogens of the neighbouring CH2 (n + 1 = 3). The fragments CH3CH2-, -COO- and -CH3 give CH3CH2COOCH3, methyl propanoate.

questions.question: Compound E is methyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH3 (molecular ion at m/z 88). Its mass spectrum has a peak at m/z 57. Suggest the formula of the ion responsible for this peak and write an equation for its formation from the molecular ion. [H = 1, C = 12, O = 16]
questions.answer: CH3CH2CO+ (m/z 57); [CH3CH2COOCH3]+• -> CH3CH2CO+ + •OCH3
steps: Mass of CH3CH2CO+ = 3 x 12 + 5 x 1 + 16 = 57, which matches the peak.
The molecular ion fragments by loss of the •OCH3 radical (mass 31): [CH3CH2COOCH3]+• -> CH3CH2CO+ + •OCH3. Only the positive ion is detected.
